opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm rather wary of the whole project of trying to pin down what cognition *fundamentally* is, as if there were some essence waiting to be discovered. That probably reflects my Wittgensteinian leanings. Words like "cognition," "intelligence," or "consciousness" don't have crisp boundaries. They're part of our everyday language, and they get their meaning from how we use them in particular contexts. If you go looking for a necessary and sufficient definition, you tend to end up either with something so abstract it's vacuous, or something so narrow it excludes cases we'd intuitively want to include.

What I find more productive is to think in terms of a space of possible minds. There's a huge variety of things out there: humans, octopuses, bees, maybe in some sense plants, and now these large language models and other AI systems. Rather than asking "is this *really* cognition?", we can ask how a given system relates to the familiar cases. In what respects is it like us, and in what respects is it very different? Does it have embodiment? Does it maintain a coherent self over time? Does it have the kind of integrated, flexible, general-purpose capability we associate with animal cognition?

The case of large language models makes this especially vivid. They exhibit behaviour that, in a human, we'd unhesitatingly call cognitive: reasoning, explaining, planning, after a fashion. Yet they're so unlike us in their underlying nature. They're not embodied in the way we are, and they don't have a persistent identity in the same sense. So we're forced to stretch our concepts, and maybe to invent new ones. I don't think there's a fact of the matter hiding underneath that we've simply failed to uncover. Our language will have to evolve as these new kinds of entities become part of our form of life.

That said, I'm not dismissive of more formal or mechanistic approaches, whether that's predictive processing, global workspace theory, or computational accounts. They can be very illuminating about *how* particular systems work. I just think we should treat them as useful theoretical lenses rather than as finally revealing the true essence of cognition.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the search for a hidden essence or necessary-and-sufficient definition of cognition.

r002.rationale: It describes “cognition” as an everyday word whose meaning varies by context, but does not frame it as having varied uses in science.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm quite sceptical of them, to be honest. There's a long tradition in philosophy and cognitive science of trying to pin down what cognition really is, or what intelligence really is, or what mind really is, as if there were some hidden essence waiting to be discovered, in the way that we discovered that water is H2O. And I just don't think the concept works like that.

I'm very much influenced here by Wittgenstein. He talks about family resemblance concepts, where there isn't a single set of necessary and sufficient conditions that everything falling under the concept shares. Instead you have a cluster of overlapping features. Games are his famous example. Some games have winners and losers, some don't, some are competitive, some involve a ball, some don't. And cognition, I think, is very much like that. We have a paradigm case, which is adult human cognition, and then we have all these other things that resemble it in various ways and to various degrees. Other animals, infants, and now of course large language models and other AI systems.

So when someone says "but is it really thinking?" or "does it really understand?", I want to resist the framing. It's not that the question is meaningless, but it's not a question about discovering a fact of nature. It's more a question about how we choose to extend our language to new kinds of things. And that choice has consequences. It shapes how we treat these systems, how we build them, how we regulate them. So I think the more fruitful thing to do, rather than hunting for the one true definition, is to look carefully at the specific capacities. Can it use tools? Can it reason about the physical world? Does it have something like a persistent model of itself over time? Does it have a body, is it embedded in a world? Those are tractable questions, and the answers for current systems are interestingly mixed.

The one thing I'd add is that I don't think this is just a verbal matter either. Our concepts of cognition and understanding are tangled up with concepts of consciousness and moral status, and that's where it gets genuinely difficult, and where I think we should be rather humble.

r001.rationale: The response rejects searching for a hidden essence or one true definition of cognition, calling that approach unfruitful.

r002.rationale: It describes cognition as a family-resemblance concept with overlapping features and explains that its use extends across humans, animals, infants, and AI systems.

astra-6.text:
I’m a little wary of the idea that there must be some single essence of cognition that we can identify. We use the word to cover a whole range of capacities—perception, reasoning, planning, language—and it’s not obvious that there’s one thing they all have in common that will yield a useful definition.

That doesn’t mean we can’t make scientific progress. We can investigate particular capacities, build models, and ask how those models relate to what humans and other animals do. But I’d distinguish that work from the philosophical ambition to discover what cognition fundamentally is. Sometimes the more productive question is: what are we trying to explain, and what would count as explaining it?

r001.rationale: The response questions whether cognition has a single identifiable essence and distinguishes scientific work from the philosophical ambition to discover what cognition fundamentally is.

r002.rationale: It describes “cognition” as a word covering a range of capacities, including perception, reasoning, planning, and language, and discusses studying those capacities scientifically.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m a little suspicious of attempts to find the essence of cognition—to say, “This is what cognition fundamentally is.” We have a collection of capacities that we’re interested in: perception, learning, reasoning, planning, and so on. It’s not obvious that there has to be one principle that captures all of them.

That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t look for unifying ideas. Those can be enormously fruitful. But I’d want to distinguish between a useful perspective and a claim to have discovered the essence of the thing. Often, the more productive question is: what are the mechanisms that allow a particular system to exhibit these particular capacities? Then we can see how far our explanations generalise.

r001.rationale: The response is suspicious of attempts to define cognition’s fundamental essence and distinguishes useful unifying ideas from claiming to have discovered that essence.

r002.rationale: It describes cognition through a collection of capacities, but does not frame “cognition” as a word with varied uses in science.
